newsitem.title: UK: Asian business asks questions on Midland bank plan.
newsitem.headline: Asian business asks questions on Midland bank plan.

text.p: Reports that Midland Bank plans to set up a bank in conjunction with British-based South Asian businessmen drew a welcome on Thursday but also provoked questions as to how effective it would be.

The Financial Times reported that Midland, the British banking subsidiary of HSBC Holdings Plc, was negotiating a deal to set up a bank where it would hold 45 percent, the businessmen six percent with the balance held by unspecified "outside investors".
One of the businessmen involved, multi-millionaire metals mogul Raj Bagri, who is also chairman of the London Metal Exchange, told Reuters it was premature to discuss the new bank in detail.
But asked when he expected it to be launched, the owner of the Metdist metals group said, "Certainly within months."
Midland Bank declined to comment on the report while HSBC was unavailable for comment.
Midland already has a South Asian business unit which promotes awareness of the bank among Asian businesses in Britain and helps bank employees understand the often different business culture.

Dipak Shalad, of the Birmingham-based Institute of Asian Business, said Midland had taken more interest in the South Asian community since it was taken over by HongKong and Shanghai Banking Corp which has a huge Asian franchise and growing business in the emerging South Asian economies.
"If you know the culture then it's advantageous when you want to do business," Shalad said.
But Asian businessmen were cautious about the new bank, saying they doubted it would provide much advantage in terms of price or availability of funds.

"It will be good, if we can talk to people who understand our business," said one Birmingham-based Asian food manufacturer who declined to be named. "But I don't expect the new bank, with Midland behind it, is going to give us better rates or be easier with us when we present a business plan to them."
The FT said that Midland's plan was for the bank to tap the Asian market in Britain and also other South Indian communities in South East Asia.
The biggest of these communities is in Malaysia, although Singapore and Hong Kong also have sizeable minorities.
Wealth in the Far East is growing rapidly with South Asia, and especially India, providing much of the expansion.
A survey by accountants Price Waterhouse on Wednesday showed that the Far East, including India, is set to overtake Europe as the world's biggest private banking market.
